roots.label: PIE horse word
roots.description: The PIE horse noun *h₁éḱwos is represented by separate Scottish Gaelic, Iranian and Greek route colours. Scottish Gaelic each continues Proto-Celtic *ekʷos via Old Irish ech. Iranian asp/asb/hesp words have their own histories. Greek learned ίππος continues Ancient Greek ἵππος and coexists with everyday άλογο. These selected forms are not an exhaustive list of surviving reflexes; Latin equus is another. Stripes show coexisting word origins rather than separate language territories.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: ASB i., Iranian horse terminology
Wiktionary: Scottish Gaelic each, via Old Irish ech and Proto-Celtic *ekʷos
Wiktionary: Greek ίππος, another surviving PIE horse-word reflex
Wiktionary: Latin equus, inherited PIE horse noun
Ivanov (1999), Comparative Notes, PDF p. 36: Talysh, Gilyan and Mazandarani horse forms
Cathcart (2015), Iranian Dialectology and Dialectometry, p. 135: Mazandarani asb

routes.label: Scottish Gaelic route
routes.description: The displayed modern word each is Scottish Gaelic. Its ancestor *ekʷos is reconstructed Proto-Celtic, not a Scottish Gaelic word: PIE *h₁éḱwos → Proto-Celtic *ekʷos → Old Irish ech → Scottish Gaelic each.

routes.label: Iranian route
routes.description: PIE *h₁éḱwos → Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćwas → Proto-Iranian *Hácwah → the selected asp/asb/hesp forms. Individual histories include Iranian-internal borrowing. Gilaki, Iranian Talysh and Mazandarani asb are separately documented regional forms. The shared origin colour does not imply that each selected form has an uninterrupted inheritance history: Iranian-internal borrowing is possible.

routes.label: Greek inherited / learned route
routes.description: PIE *h₁éḱwos → Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos) → learned Modern Greek ίππος. This coexists with everyday άλογο, which has a separate origin.

roots.label: Caballus word-family
roots.description: The caballus / *kaballos word-family is shown under one shared heading with three separately coloured routes. Romance words continue Latin caballus; Albanian kalë is borrowed through Latin. Irish capall, Manx cabbyl and Welsh ceffyl belong to the related Celtic word-family, with disputed early borrowing directions and deeper origin. The shared heading does not assert that every Celtic term descends directly from Latin. This family is distinct from Latin equus, the inherited PIE horse noun.

sources.title: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary: caballus

routes.label: Romance route
routes.description: Latin caballus → the Romance horse words shown here, including Spanish caballo, French cheval and Italian cavallo.

routes.label: Celtic route
routes.description: The related caballos word-family in Celtic: Irish capall, Manx cabbyl and Welsh ceffyl. Early forms and borrowing directions differ by word and remain disputed; this row does not make all three direct descendants of Latin caballus.

routes.label: Albanian route
routes.description: A Latin loan into Albanian: caballus → Proto-Albanian *kəβal → Albanian kalë.

roots.label: Germanic
roots.description: English horse and Scots horse descend through Old English hors from Germanic *hrussą (also reconstructed *hursą). Proposed deeper derivations exist, including a connection with running, but are not certain. This is not *h₁éḱwos.

roots.label: Late Latin
roots.description: German Pferd, Dutch paard and Luxembourgish Päerd continue a borrowing of Late Latin paraverēdus, a substitute post horse. It combines Greek para- with Latin verēdus, a Gaulish loan. The whole word is not the ordinary inherited Germanic horse noun.

roots.label: Germanic
roots.description: The Scandinavian hest/häst/hestur set descends from Germanic *hangistaz / *hanhistaz. West Frisian hynder is a compound based on the cognate hynst plus dier. Northern Sámi heasta and Greenlandic hiisti are Scandinavian borrowings. Their shared colour follows the word history rather than language family.

sources.title: Matsumoto Ryo, Horse in Uralic, Linguistic Atlas of Asia and Africa, p.147

roots.label: Slavic
roots.description: The selected Slavic konj/koń/kinʹ forms belong to the inherited Proto-Slavic horse set. Its deeper origin is debated, so no definite connection to the PIE *h₁éḱwos set is drawn. Russian also has конь; the common generic лошадь is selected separately.

roots.label: Turkic → Russian
roots.description: Russian лошадь comes through Old East Slavic лоша from a Turkic source, compared with Tatar алаша and Chuvash лаша. The donor variety and deeper history are not fixed here. This set is distinct from Turkic at.

roots.label: Lithuanian
roots.description: Lithuanian arklys is an agentive derivative connected with arklas, plough: a ploughing animal. It is not the same selected word as Latvian zirgs, although Lithuanian also has the cognate žirgas.

roots.label: Baltic
roots.description: Latvian zirgs continues a Baltic horse word, cognate with Lithuanian žirgas. The map selects Lithuanian arklys separately rather than merging the two countries by family.

roots.label: Celtic
roots.description: Breton marc’h and Cornish margh continue Celtic *markos. Its relationship to Germanic *marhaz and its deeper origin are debated. It is distinct from Celtic *ekwos, which survives in Scottish Gaelic each.

roots.label: Greek
roots.description: Modern Greek άλογο comes from the neuter of Ancient Greek ἄλογος, unreasoning or speechless, through its use for horse. Greek also has ίππος from the PIE horse word, but that is not the common label selected here.

roots.label: Armenian
roots.description: Armenian ձի continues Old Armenian ji, compared with Vedic háya, horse, from a proposed Indo-European formation *ǵʰéyos associated with driving or impelling. It is kept separate from the regular *h₁éḱwos horse noun.

roots.label: Armenian loan into Romani
roots.description: Romani grast, gras, gra and graj are cognate forms of an early Armenian loan. The selected Romanian grast and German Sinti graj share this origin colour. This is a distinct word history from Armenian dzi on the map. Different Romani varieties are not assumed to have unrelated horse nouns simply because they live in different countries.

sources.title: Halwachs, Klinge and Schrammel-Leber (2013), RomIdent Paper 3, p. 10 table 2: Romani horse cognates and Armenian loan origin
Manchester Romani Project: Early Romani, Armenian loan grast
ArmDict English–Armenian dictionary: beast of burden, գրաստ

roots.label: Ossetian
roots.description: Ossetian бӕх continues Alanic *bæx. Its deeper ancestry is unresolved here; belonging to Iranian does not make this noun a descendant of the asp/asb horse set.

roots.label: Finnic
roots.description: Finnish hevonen and Estonian hobune continue diminutive formations of the Finnic horse word *hëpo; Karelian and Veps hebo continue the shorter form. A Germanic or other Indo-European source has been proposed, but no secure deeper link is asserted.

roots.label: Ugric
roots.description: Hungarian ló (stem lov-), Khanty ԓов (Kazym łow, often simplified lov) and Northern Mansi лув (luw) share the inherited Ugric horse-word set. The Hungarian etymological dictionary reconstructs *luβɜ or *luγɜ. Its earlier donor and remote origin remain unresolved; no definite deeper Indo-European ancestry is asserted.

sources.title: HUN-REN, Új magyar etimológiai szótár: ló, Ugric inheritance and Khanty/Mansi cognates
V. N. Solovar 2014, Khanty–Russian Dictionary (Kazym dialect), p. 154: ԓов, horse
Ob-Ugric Institute, short Mansi–Russian dictionary: лув, horse

roots.label: Permic
roots.description: Udmurt вал and Komi вӧв are cognates continuing Permic *vɔ̇l, compared with a wider *wälɜ animal-word set. No direct connection with Hungarian ló or Finnic *hëpo is asserted.

roots.label: Mari
roots.description: Meadow Mari имне is cognate with Hill Mari имни. This attested Mari set is shown without an invented common Uralic horse root.

sources.title: Matsumoto Ryo, Horse in Uralic, p.147

roots.label: Turkic → Samoyedic
roots.description: Tundra Nenets юно continues the Samoyedic *juntå horse set, traced to Old Turkic yunt. It is distinct from the Turkic at and yïlkï sets. Forest Nenets has a different Ugric loan; this map uses a Tundra Nenets reference.

sources.title: COPIUS, Samoyedic historical phonology: *juntå → Tundra Nenets juna/juno
Matsumoto Ryo, Horse in Uralic, p.147

roots.label: Basque
roots.description: Basque zaldi is an old Basque horse word. Its remote origin is not resolved by the present comparison and no shared PIE ancestry is asserted.

roots.label: Arabic
roots.description: The selected Arabic citation form حصان means horse or stallion and belongs to the root ḥ-ṣ-n. It is distinct from the sus/susya set in Hebrew and Aramaic. Regional vowels vary; these labels are representative forms, not an inventory of all local synonyms.

roots.label: Arabic ʕawd horse word
roots.description: Maghrebi Arabic عود is represented by Algerian ʿūd and Moroccan ʿawd. The proposed earlier Arabic sense is a camel trained for riding. Kossmann (2013, pp. 149–150) explicitly derives Kabyle aɛawḏiw / aɛudiw from Maghrebi Arabic ɛǝwd(a), so the Kabyle loan shares this origin colour. These are distinct from the ḥiṣān and faras horse-word sets.

sources.title: Lameen Souag (2002), The Algerian Arabic of Dellys: ʕud / ʕwad, horse, appendix p. 33
Wiktionary: Algerian Arabic عود, from Arabic ʕawd, a camel trained for riding
Kossmann (2013), The Arabic Influence on Northern Berber, pp. 149–150: horse words and Arabic loans
Darija Dictionary: عود, horse, with native audio

roots.label: Arabic faras set
roots.description: The written Hassaniya horse word فرس is documented in the Peace Corps handbook, p. 249. It belongs to the Arabic faras horse-word set, distinct from ḥiṣān and ʿawd. The map uses frs as a consonant-only transliteration because the exact local vocalization has not been verified; it must not be read as an IPA pronunciation or silently replaced by the standard Arabic reading.

sources.title: Peace Corps (1979), Hassaniya Arabic handbook, p. 249: written فرس, horse

roots.label: Hebrew & Aramaic
roots.description: Hebrew sus and the selected Aramaic and Mandaic words belong to the old sūs/sūsyā horse-word set, also compared with Akkadian sīsû. Early borrowing and ultimate origins are disputed; they are not linked automatically to Arabic ḥiṣān or PIE *h₁éḱwos.

roots.label: Arabic → Maltese
roots.description: Maltese żiemel comes from Arabic zāmil, horse or wild ass, related to zāmila, a load-carrying she-camel. The semantic history involves a pack animal; this is not a reflex of the sus or ḥiṣān sets.

roots.label: Berber
roots.description: Central Atlas Tamazight ayis, Tachelhit ayyis and Rif yis belong to the inherited Berber horse-word set. Kossmann distinguishes them from Arabic-derived horse words and from the agmar set. No speculative remote Indo-European etymology is asserted.

sources.title: Kossmann (2013), The Arabic Influence on Northern Berber, pp. 149–150: horse words and Arabic loans
Kossmann, WOLD Tarifiyt: yis, horse, Common Berber; no evidence of borrowing

roots.label: Berber agmar set
roots.description: Nafusi agmár and Ghadames aǧmar are members of the Berber GMR horse-word set, separate from ayis / yis and from Arabic horse loans. The comparison stops at this Berber set; a Latin or other remote origin is not asserted.

sources.title: Marijn van Putten, Nefusa Text: The story of the wild animals, agmár, horse, analysing Beguinot 1942
Kossmann (2013), The Arabic Influence on Northern Berber, pp. 149–150: horse words and Arabic loans

roots.label: Turkic
roots.description: The at/ot set continues the Common Turkic horse word. Uzbek ot reflects the same set. Kazakh has at too, but the common species/livestock noun жылқы is selected separately.

roots.label: Turkic
roots.description: Kazakh жылқы continues the Turkic yïlkï livestock/horse-herd term, related to the word for year or age in the cited analysis. It is a different lexical origin from at.

roots.label: Kartvelian
roots.description: Georgian ცხენი continues Old Georgian ცხენი and is compared with Mingrelian and Laz forms in the Kartvelian *cxen- set. No PIE horse etymology is asserted.

roots.label: Nakh
roots.description: Chechen and Ingush говр continue a Nakh horse-word set. The deeper history is not resolved here.

roots.label: Circassian
roots.description: Adyghe and Kabardian шы continue the Circassian horse-word set. It is kept separate from the selected Northeast Caucasian words.

roots.label: Avar
roots.description: Avar чу is the documented horse noun. Proposed early Indo-Iranian connections in Caucasian horse terminology are not treated as settled by this map.

roots.label: Dargwa
roots.description: Dargwa урчи is the documented horse noun. An early Iranian source is proposed in the cited etymological material, but its chronology and relationship to neighbouring Caucasian words are left unresolved here.

roots.label: Lezgian
roots.description: Lezgian шив is an attested horse noun. Its remote relationship to other Caucasian and Iranian words is not established here.

roots.label: Lak
roots.description: Lak чву is an attested horse noun. It is shown as a local comparison set rather than assigned an unsupported deep ancestor.

roots.label: Mongolic
roots.description: Kalmyk мөрн in the horse sense continues Mongolic *morin. A homograph means river and has a different origin; that river etymology does not apply to this map.

roots.label: Indo-Aryan ghota set
roots.description: Aleppo Domari agōra belongs to the inherited Indo-Aryan ghōṭa horse-word set documented by Herin. It is distinct from the Armenian grast loan found in Romani varieties, and is not assigned to the PIE h1ekwos set merely because Domari is Indo-European. Its more remote ancestry is not asserted.

sources.title: Herin (2012), The Domari Language of Aleppo, p. 17: agor-es / agor-en from Indo-Aryan ghota; p. 2: Damascus community
Herin (2016), Elements of Domari Dialectology, p. 46 table 7: northern (a)gora, southern gori
Matras and Kelzi (2024), The Dom language of Aleppo, pp. 9–10: agora in the authors transcription; pp. 4–5: diaspora and source-speaker limits

languages.notes: Agōra follows the northern citation (a)gōra in Herin (2016, p. 46); the stem agōr- is directly attested in Aleppo by Herin (2012). Matras and Kelzi (2024) use agorà; their à marks vowel quality rather than just stress. Scholarly Latin transcription is retained rather than inventing an Arabic spelling. The Aleppo anchor is a documented reference community; the 2024 source describes extensive post-2011 dispersal, so this is not a current population boundary. The additional Sayyida Zainab/Damascus dot records community presence in older sources, not a verified contemporary Damascus horse word. Groome’s Damascus-origin 1881 material contains historical unsegmented horse phrases, which are preserved in the audit rather than made into a modern lemma. Domari and European Romani are distinct languages.

methodology.title: Lexical and etymological method
methodology.scope: 128 selected horse word / regional reference entries across Europe and neighbouring regions, including coexisting words and dispersed minority communities.
methodology.comparison: Colours follow displayed etymological routes. The PIE horse noun has separate Scottish Gaelic, Iranian and Greek routes. Caballus has separate Romance, Celtic and Albanian routes. In Greece, Russia and Kazakhstan, diagonal stripes show coexisting words with different origins in the same language area; the stripe proportions are decorative, not usage statistics. Small colour bars beneath those word labels identify their respective roots.
methodology.chains: Chains are schematic, not complete dated sound histories. Borrowing and derivation are noted; shared colour does not imply direct inheritance. Asterisks mark reconstructed, unattested forms. Alternate words keep their own origin chains; geographic coexistence is not a claim of cognacy.
methodology.uncertainty: An asterisk marks a reconstructed form. The legend uses “loan ?” for a possible borrowing. Other uncertainties, including disputed deeper origins and early borrowing directions, are explained in the entry notes rather than abbreviated in the legend. The origin of caballus/*kaballos and the deeper origin of English horse are disputed. Finnic *hëpo is not automatically merged with PIE *h₁éḱwos. Early Iranian relationships proposed for Caucasian horse words remain proposals. No indigenous Canarian horse word was verified; that label and its historical island-reference fill are omitted, leaving the modern Spanish reference layer. The former snow gloss tener? is not reused.
methodology.standards: Non-Latin labels retain native scripts with a parenthesized romanized reading beneath. Scholarly Latin transcriptions are used where no reliable native spelling was checked. Romanizations are not IPA. Northern Luri uses a local speaker wordlist; the Iraqi reference ḥiṣān is also attested in a Baghdadi Arabic study, without asserting uniform regional vowels. Mandaic is literary/liturgical. The Maaloula label uses an editorial Syriac rendering of Arnold’s attested sūsča, with the spelling convention and its limits documented in that entry.
methodology.sources: Wiktionary is a community-edited secondary reference. Entries are linked individually, with institutional and primary lexical sources for key unusual varieties. Research records and the source catalog retain the distinction between checked forms and unresolved deeper histories.
